author: Carlos Martinez
title: Button Boxes and Handbrakes for Rally and Drift in iRacing
description: Add button boxes and hydraulic handbrakes to control rally and drift cars without sacrificing wheel real estate or FFB clarity.

sections.p: Rally and drift cars in iRacing demand inputs that standard wheels cannot handle cleanly. A sequential shifter, turbo anti-lag, differential adjustments, and a handbrake each need their own control, and they all carry weight during a race. Button boxes and dedicated handbrakes move those functions off your steering wheel, freeing up button real estate and letting you use a lighter, more responsive wheel setup.

This is not a cosmetic upgrade. When you have a button box, you can keep your rally car's handbrake on a physical lever instead of a wheel button, which means more precise brake modulation, faster reflexes, and no accidental inputs during aggressive steering inputs. The same logic applies to drift cars that use paddle shifters or rotary dial shifters: a dedicated handbrake gives you a third hand for car control.

A button box is a secondary control panel, usually mounted to the left of your seat or on a separate stand, that holds switches, rotaries, and buttons for functions you use less frequently or need quick access to outside your wheel. In rally, that includes anti-lag, differential bias, brake balance adjustments, and sometimes a clutch if you run manual starts. In drift, a button box can hold turbo boost controls or display settings.

The primary advantage is modularity. You are not competing for wheel real estate with 12 extra buttons that obscure your grip or add weight. A wheel designed for grip and FFB feedback stays lean. A button box sits in a fixed position where your left hand can find controls by muscle memory alone, without looking.

list: Rotary dials for multi-position settings like differential lock percentage or fuel mixture
Toggle switches for on-off functions like anti-lag, traction control modes, or pit limiter
Momentary buttons for quick actions like turbo deployment or brake balance adjustment
Encoder knobs for smooth adjustment of brake or throttle bias while driving
LED feedback to show which mode or setting is currently active

sections.tip: A button box does not replace a handbrake. It complements one. Use your button box for settings and modes you adjust mid-race, and use a dedicated handbrake for the actual car control input.
sections.tipLabel: Button Box and Handbrake Work Together

sections.p: A dedicated handbrake in iRacing rally and drift is as essential as pedals. iRacing registers the handbrake as an analog input, meaning the game reads how hard you pull or push it, not just whether it is on or off. A hydraulic handbrake mimics real car behavior: it holds pressure as long as you hold the lever, then releases fully when you let go. A spring-return handbrake (sometimes called a cable handbrake) pulls back to neutral on its own.

For rally, most drivers prefer a cable-return or spring-loaded handbrake because it matches the feel of rallying with one hand on the steering wheel and quick handbrake taps for tight hairpins. For drift, a hydraulic handbrake that holds pressure gives you more control over sustained drifts where you modulate the brake to hold the angle. Neither is objectively better: the difference is feel and what your muscle memory expects.

list: Hydraulic handbrakes hold pressure and require an active release. They let you modulate brake pressure mid-action and suit sustained drifts or multi-stage corners.
Spring-return handbrakes snap back to neutral after you release them. They suit rally where you need quick, clean inputs and do not want to hold the lever.
Cable-based systems sit between the two: they return slowly to neutral and are common in budget rigs.
Load cell handbrakes (rare, high-end) read the force you apply, not just position, for ultra-fine control.

sections.h2: Choosing Button Box and Handbrake Brands

sections.p: Popular button box makers include SimXperience, Heusinkveld, and smaller specialists like NGRS. Most are unbranded aluminum or 3D-printed frames with mechanical switches and rotary encoders that you can program via USB. Cost ranges from roughly 100 to 400 USD depending on the number of inputs and build quality. A good starting point is a simple 8 to 12-button box with one or two rotary dials: enough to handle anti-lag, differential, and brake balance without overwhelming your setup.

Handbrakes come from Heusinkveld, SimXperience, Fanatec, and boutique makers. Hydraulic systems cost roughly 300 to 600 USD; mechanical cable or spring-return systems cost 150 to 300 USD. Heusinkveld makes the most common reference model, the Ultimate Plus, which uses a master cylinder and brake fluid to simulate hydraulic feel. It is a heavy, immobile unit that bolts to your cockpit frame and can handle real force without slipping.

list: Heusinkveld Ultimate Plus: hydraulic, expensive, immobile, most realistic feel
SimXperience (various models): compact, adjustable spring rates, suits portable rigs
Fanatec ClubSport Handbrake: lighter, hybrid feel, integrates with Fanatec ecosystem
DIY mechanical handbrakes: budget option using PVC, springs, and potentiometers

sections.p: A button box should live within arm's reach of your steering wheel, usually mounted to the left side of your seat or on a separate stand between your legs. If you have a full cockpit frame, you can bolt it to an aluminum profile or mount it on the existing rig. The goal is accessibility without distraction: your left hand should know where every button and dial is by touch alone.

A handbrake mounts to the left side of your seat, typically where your left leg would be in a real rally or drift car. It needs a stable base so pulling or pushing it does not shift your rig. A cockpit frame is crucial here: a loose stand will wobble and ruin your inputs. If you are on a budget cockpit, you may need to weld or clamp the handbrake mount yourself.

Both devices connect to your PC via USB, usually to a hub or directly to the motherboard. Make sure your USB hub is powered; unpowered hubs can cause dropout during intense inputs. Test all connections before a race.

olist: Mount the handbrake to your cockpit frame on the left side, 15 to 20 degrees forward of your hip for natural lever reach
Mount the button box on the left armrest or on a separate aluminum stand, within 12 inches of your left hand
Connect both devices to a powered USB hub, not to your motherboard directly if you have other peripherals
Assign buttons and axes in the iRacing control menu and test each one in a practice session before racing
Cover or tape any unused buttons to avoid accidental presses during bumpy corners

sections.p: Most button boxes use software like Leo Bodnar's BBI32U or custom firmware that maps each switch and dial to a USB HID input. You assign these in iRacing's control menu just as you would wheel buttons. The handbrake shows up as an analog axis, so you calibrate its min and max travel and check the dead zone.

For rally, your button box should include at least anti-lag toggle, differential lock (or differential bias adjustment), and brake balance offset. A second dial for fuel mixture is useful in endurance rallies. Assign them to buttons or rotaries that make physical sense: a rotary dial for bias feels more natural than a momentary button that steps through percentages.

For drift, your button box handles turbo boost, nitrous, or differential adjustment. The handbrake is your primary control: bind it to a single axis and tune the deadzone so small inputs do not trigger accidental brakes. Drift setups often run very low handbrake linearity so small movements give subtle lock, and large pulls give hard lock.

sections.tip: Test your button box and handbrake calibration in a practice session on a small oval or dirt track first. Iron out any drift in calibration or unexpected axis reversals before you enter a league race.

sections.h2: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

sections.p: One frequent mistake is mounting the handbrake too far forward or at the wrong angle. If you have to reach or bend your wrist to grip it, you will lose smooth modulation and fatigue faster. Handbrakes should sit where your natural resting arm angle can grab and move it. Test by sitting in your rig with your steering wheel in position and finding where your left arm naturally lands.

Another is cramming too many buttons into the button box. More inputs do not make you faster. Stick to functions you actually adjust mid-race. Anti-lag, differential, and brake balance are the core set. Everything else can wait for practice or a pit stop.

Using a powered USB hub connected to your motherboard instead of a wall power supply can cause dropout. Handbrakes and button boxes draw more power than small wheels because they have motors or solenoids in some cases. If your inputs cut out during a race, check your USB power first. A cheap powered hub is worth it.

list: Mount the handbrake at a natural arm angle. If you have to reach or flex your wrist, raise or move it closer.
Start with 8 to 12 buttons and add more only if you use every one in a race.
Connect to a powered USB hub, not an unpowered one or directly to the motherboard.
Calibrate every device in practice before entering a league race.
Label or color-code buttons and dials so you can find them by touch in the dark.

sections.p: A button box is not mandatory for rally or drift. You can assign functions to wheel buttons or use the numeric pad on your keyboard. But if you race rally or drift regularly, a dedicated handbrake and a small button box (8 to 12 buttons, roughly 150 to 300 USD combined for budget options) will improve your consistency and free up mental load. You will stop fumbling for buttons and start focusing on the racing.

A high-end hydraulic handbrake is expensive (300 to 600 USD) and only worth it if you compete in formal drift or rally leagues where the extra realism and modulation matter. For casual racing or practice, a mechanical spring-return handbrake does the job just fine and costs half as much.
The real win is ergonomics and repeatability. When your hands know exactly where to find the handbrake and each button, you stop thinking about inputs and start thinking about racing.

faqs.q: Do I need a button box if I only race rally occasionally?
faqs.a: No. If you rally once a month, wheel buttons or keyboard binds are sufficient. A button box makes sense if you race rally or drift weekly and want faster, more ergonomic inputs.

faqs.q: Can I use a keyboard or gamepad for handbrake instead of a dedicated device?
faqs.a: Technically yes, but it is clumsy. A keyboard key is on-off, and a gamepad trigger lacks the analog precision you need for drift braking modulation. A dedicated handbrake, even a cheap mechanical one, gives you continuous analog control.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a hydraulic and spring-return handbrake for drift?
faqs.a: A hydraulic handbrake holds pressure as long as you hold the lever, letting you modulate brake pressure mid-drift. A spring-return handbrake snaps back to neutral after release, which is better for rally where you need quick taps. For drift, hydraulic gives more control; for rally, spring-return feels more natural.

faqs.q: How much does a decent button box and handbrake setup cost?
faqs.a: A simple 8-button box costs roughly 100 to 150 USD. A mechanical spring-return handbrake costs 150 to 300 USD. A hydraulic handbrake costs 300 to 600 USD. Total: budget 250 to 750 USD for a solid setup, or 100 to 200 USD if you go DIY for the button box and use a mechanical handbrake.
